title: How to Fix Bubbling Paint on Drywall for Good
description: Bubbling paint on drywall means the film lost its bond. Find the cause, then cut out, skim, prime, and repaint the wall so the bubbles do not come back.
excerpt: Paint bubbles on drywall mean the film has lost its bond. Find the cause first, then cut, skim, prime, and repaint so they stay gone.
h1: How to Fix Bubbling Paint on Drywall for Good
heroIntro: Popping a paint bubble and dabbing on more paint feels like a fix, but the bubble usually comes back next to the old one. Lasting repairs start with figuring out why the paint let go.

questions: Why is my wall paint bubbling?
How do you fix bubbling paint on drywall?
Will paint bubbles go away on their own?
Do I need primer over joint compound?

sections.h2: What causes paint to bubble on drywall
body: A bubble or blister means the paint film has separated from the surface beneath it. That happens for a short list of reasons, and the fix depends on which one you have.
bullets: Moisture from a leak, a bathroom without proper ventilation, condensation on an exterior wall, or high indoor humidity.
Unprimed joint compound: compound is porous and powdery, and paint applied directly over it can lose its grip, especially over large patches.
Dust left from sanding drywall or patches before painting.
Painting over a surface with grease, soap residue, or nicotine film, common in kitchens and older homes.
Latex paint applied directly over glossy oil-based paint without deglossing or a bonding primer.
Heavy coats or painting in high heat, which can skin the surface while solvent or water is still trapped underneath.

body: Slice one bubble open with a utility knife and look at what is underneath. If there is water or the drywall paper is damp or stained, you have a moisture problem; find and fix it before anything else. A cheap pin moisture meter or a non-invasive meter helps here. If the bubble reveals bare, chalky joint compound, the issue is adhesion over an unprimed patch. If there is an older layer of paint underneath that looks glossy, you are dealing with incompatible coatings.

Look at the pattern too. Bubbles clustered near the ceiling of a bathroom point to steam. Bubbles on an exterior wall after storms point to water entering from outside, which can be a siding, window, or roof issue; see hidden moisture damage behind siding. Bubbles only over patches point to prep. Small bubbles that appear while you are rolling and then flatten are just roller foam and are a different, minor issue.
One caution: if the home was built before 1978, test the paint for lead before sanding or scraping large areas, and if you are working on textured ceilings, test for asbestos before disturbing them.

bullets: Fix the cause first: repair leaks, improve ventilation, and let the wall dry completely.
Scrape away every loose and bubbled area until the paint edges are firmly attached.
If the drywall paper has torn or fuzzed, seal it with a shellac-based or oil-based primer before patching, or the moisture in the compound will bubble the paper.
Skim the area with joint compound, let it dry, and sand it smooth and flat. Feather the edges wide so the patch disappears.
Remove sanding dust with a vacuum and a damp cloth.
Prime with a bonding or stain-blocking primer appropriate to the cause: a stain-blocker where there was water staining, a bonding primer over glossy paint, and a drywall primer-sealer over compound.
Repaint the entire wall, corner to corner, rather than just the patch, so the sheen and color match.

body: The words get used interchangeably, but they hint at different stages. Fresh bubbles that appear within hours of painting usually involve trapped moisture or air during application, or paint applied over a surface that was too warm, damp, or dirty. Blisters that show up weeks or months later, especially after a leak or a humid stretch, are a moisture story. Once blisters break and the edges curl, you have peeling, and the loss of adhesion has usually spread beyond what you can see.

Run your putty knife gently under the edge of the damaged area. If the paint lifts easily several inches away from the visible bubble, plan on scraping a larger area than you expected. That extra scraping now is what keeps the repair from outlining itself in a few months.

sections.h2: Choosing the right paint for the room
body: In bathrooms and laundry rooms, use a paint rated for high-humidity rooms with mildew-resistant properties, usually in satin or semi-gloss, which sheds moisture better than flat. In kitchens, a scrubbable eggshell or satin handles grease and cleaning. For living spaces, a quality interior acrylic is fine once the surface is right. Our guide to choosing a paint finish for every room goes room by room.

sections.h2: When it is more than a paint problem
body: Some bubbling is a symptom of something bigger. If the drywall is soft, crumbly, or sagging, if the stain keeps growing, or if you smell mustiness, the board itself may be wet or moldy and should be cut out and replaced after the water source is fixed. Repeated bubbling on an exterior wall can mean water is entering the wall cavity. In those cases a painting repair alone will fail, and a drywall repair that replaces damaged board is the right first step.
For broader moisture issues in Florida homes, our article on humidity and peeling paint covers ventilation and dehumidification in more detail.

Prime every patch, every time. Keep indoor relative humidity in a comfortable range, generally somewhere around 40 to 50 percent, by running the air conditioning and bathroom exhaust fans; a fan should vent outside, not into the attic, and run for a while after showers. Clean kitchen walls periodically so grease does not build up under the next coat. And give fresh paint the dry time on the label before closing a steamy bathroom door on it.

One or two small blisters on a dry wall are a manageable DIY repair with the steps above. Large areas, ceilings, recurring bubbles, water-damaged board, or anything involving possible lead or asbestos are better handled by a crew with the tools and containment to do it cleanly. faqs.q: Will paint bubbles go away on their own?
faqs.a: Small bubbles that form while rolling often flatten as the paint dries. Blisters that appear later, after the paint has dried, will not go away and need to be scraped, patched, primed, and repainted.

faqs.q: Can I just pop the bubbles and paint over them?
faqs.a: That rarely lasts. The paint around the bubble has usually lost adhesion too. Remove all loose paint, fix the cause, prime, and repaint the full wall.

faqs.q: Do I need to prime joint compound before painting?
faqs.a: Yes. Joint compound is porous and powdery. A drywall primer-sealer gives the paint something to bond to and prevents flashing and adhesion failures.

faqs.q: Why does the paint in my bathroom keep bubbling?
faqs.a: Usually steam and poor ventilation. Make sure the exhaust fan vents outdoors and runs long enough after showers, then repaint with a primer and a paint rated for bathrooms.
